# Ribbon

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

How far apart were the lowest and highest values at each date? `ribbon` draws a
filled band from a low boundary to a high one across x: a confidence band, a
spread band, the shaded region around a trend. It fills one region, the way an
[`area`](area.qmd) does. It reads a low value and a high value at each
position, the way an [`interval`](interval.qmd) does. An area fills from the
data down to a baseline at zero. A ribbon has no baseline, and both of its
edges come from the data, always through a transform. With a category on one
axis and `density`, the same mark draws a violin plot.

## A band from a range {#a-band-from-a-range}

The `gapminder_asia` table holds five Asian countries: China, India, Indonesia,
Japan and South Korea (`Korea, Rep.` in the table). Each is measured every five
years from 1952 to 2007. Did the life expectancies of those five move closer
together over the years, or further apart?
The gap between the lowest and the highest in each year answers that. A band
drawn between those two values shows every year at once, as one shape. The two
boundaries come from a transform, exactly as an interval's two extents do.
`range` reduces `y` to its minimum and maximum within each `x`, and the ribbon
fills between them. Here, the spread of life expectancy across five Asian
countries, year by year:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_asia)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The min–max spread across five Asian countries, per year")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: a ribbon derived by range, x is year, y is life."*

In each year the band's lower edge is at the lowest life expectancy of the
five, and its upper edge is at the highest. The band is the region that holds
all five. It narrows from about 26 years wide in 1952 to about 18 in 2007, so
the five countries moved closer together.

The low and high pair is the one `interval * range` draws as a **whisker**, a
line from the low value to the high one, at each x. The ribbon fills the same
pair continuously. Only the shape drawn from it changes.

## A band with a mean line {#a-band-with-a-mean-line}

On its own, a band shows the spread but not the center. A band is usually drawn
with a line for the center, such as the mean. You compose the two by layering, not by adding
an option to either mark. A `ribbon * range` for the spread, a `line * mean` for
the trend, sharing one `x` and `y`:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  ribbon * range + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.25) +
  line * mean + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy, with its min–max band")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, a ribbon derived by range and also
a line derived by mean."*

Each layer runs its own transform on the same table. `mean` reduces each year to
one point for the line, and `range` reduces the same year to a low and high pair
for the band. This is the most common ribbon plot: a trend with its uncertainty
or spread drawn around it. It is two marks the grammar already has, added with
`+`.

## A fan chart of nested bands {#a-fan-chart-of-nested-bands}

Which values of life expectancy do most countries have in each year? `gm_all`
holds all the gapminder years: every country, in every year, 142 countries in
all. A min–max band over it spans the full range of life expectancy in each
year, but only the two extreme countries set its edges. Naming two quantiles
instead gives a band that contains most of the countries. `range(0.1, 0.9)`
runs from the 10th percentile to the 90th, so it holds the middle 80% of the
countries. `range(0.25, 0.75)` holds the middle half ([A band between two
quantiles](../transforms.qmd#a-band-between-two-quantiles)). Layer two bands of
different widths to draw a **fan chart**:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_all)
```

```{r}
data(gm_all) + x(year) + y(life) +
  ribbon * range(0.1, 0.9) + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.2) +
  ribbon * range(0.25, 0.75) + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.35) +
  line * median + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Life expectancy across 142 countries, 1952 to 2007")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: x is year, y is life, a ribbon derived by range
from 0.1 to 0.9, and also a ribbon derived by range from 0.25 to 0.75, and also
a line derived by median."*

The pale band contains the middle 80% of countries. The darker one contains the
middle half, and the line is the median. This plot shows something the min–max
version cannot. The median rose from 45 years to 72, and the 90th
percentile from 67 to 80, so the distance between them fell from 22 years to 8.

The lower edges of the two bands do not rise steadily. Both lower edges, the
10th percentile and the 25th, decline between 1992 and 2002 while the median
rises throughout. A min–max band cannot show this, because its lower edge is one
country.

Each band is one more layer, so a third pair of quantiles adds a third band.
Write the widest band first, because a later layer is drawn over an earlier
one.

## Why a ribbon needs a transform {#why-a-ribbon-needs-a-transform}

A low *and* a high are two numbers, and a plain `y()` supplies one. An `area`
closes on zero: its region's other edge is zero, which the grammar supplies. A
ribbon has no such second number. Law 7, the [minimum
syllable](../design-laws.qmd#law-7-minimum-syllable), says a mark draws only
with every position it needs. For a ribbon those are an `x`, a low and a high.
Like an `interval`, it needs a transform that supplies the low and the high. Write a ribbon without one and the
engine refuses it, rather than drawing an empty panel. [What it
refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows the message.

Computing the boundaries in a transform also keeps the [channel
vocabulary](../grammar.qmd#channels-a-column-made-visible) small. The
alternative, used by ggplot2, would add `ymin` and `ymax` as two more channels
that only a few marks use. A box plot would then need five such channels, one
for each number it summarizes. With a transform instead, the same low and high
values can be drawn as a whisker, as two lines, or as a filled band.

A ribbon can take eight transforms that supply the low and the high. Six are
the **pair transforms**:
`range`, `confidence`, `deviation`, `smooth_band`, `straight_band` and
`bounds`. [Transforms](../transforms.qmd) explains each one. The other two are
`density`, over a category, and `flow`. `density` gives one curve per category, and the ribbon
draws that curve and its **mirror image** as the two boundaries. That is [the
violin](#the-violin-a-distribution-per-category), later in this chapter. `flow`
is shown in [Transforms it takes](#transforms-it-takes).

## A confidence band {#a-confidence-band}

How well is the mean life expectancy known in each year? That is a different
question from how far the five countries spread. `range` shows the full
spread. For the **uncertainty of the mean**, use
`confidence`. It computes a t-interval for the mean at each `x`, and the ribbon
fills between its two boundaries. Here is the 95% band for the same five
countries, on the right, beside the min–max band from the start of this
chapter:

```{r}
(data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) +
   y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * range")) |
  (data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * confidence(0.95) + x(year) + y(life) +
     y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * confidence(0.95)"))
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: a ribbon derived by range, x is year, y is life, beside
a ribbon derived by confidence at 95%, x is year, y is life."*

The confidence band is wide because each mean comes from only five countries.
Those five differ by more than fifteen years, so the interval around their mean
is wide. A confidence level above 0.95 draws a wider band still.

The two bands are almost the same width. That comes from having only five
values, not from the two transforms agreeing. Over the 142 countries of
`gm_all`, the 95% band in 2007 is about 4 years wide, while their range is 43
years. The plots in [Transforms it takes](#transforms-it-takes) show both. What
the band means is decided by the transform you name: `range` draws the observed
spread, and `confidence` draws the uncertainty of the mean. The mark stays the
same in both plots, exactly as it does for [`interval`](interval.qmd).

## A pre-computed band {#a-pre-computed-band}

`range`, `confidence`, `deviation`, `smooth_band` and `straight_band` compute the
band from the raw values in the table, at the moment gog draws the plot. Many bands are
computed earlier, by the analysis itself. A model's standard error, a standard
error of measurement, a bootstrap interval: each of these is computed *before
the plot*. Each gives a low value and a high one, and those two become two
columns in the table. gog draws what you computed, and it does not re-fit the
model. The `score_band` table holds one row per raw score on a test scored from
0 to 20. Each row also holds the **expected true score** for that raw score, the
score a model predicts, and the two ends of a 95% band around it. In this table
the expected true score equals the raw score, so a line through it is a
diagonal:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(score_band)
```

The ribbon reads those edge columns directly, through `bounds(lower, upper)`:

```{r}
data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + x(score) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("A pre-computed measurement band")
```

*"Given the score band: a ribbon from lower to upper, x is score."*

`bounds` is the pair transform that computes nothing. It reshapes the two
columns you give it into the same low and high pair `range` writes. The band
needs no `y()`, because the two columns *are* the boundaries. This is the one
case `range`, `confidence`, `deviation`, `smooth_band` and `straight_band` cannot
write: a band
that was computed outside the plot, before gog ever read the table.

A band like this is usually drawn together with the values it surrounds. Here
those values are the expected true scores. A dashed [`line`](line.qmd) draws
them, with a point at every raw score. The band, the line and the points are
three layers composed with `+`:

```{r}
data(score_band) + x(score) + y(expected) +
  ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.18) +
  line + style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.4, pattern = "dashed") +
  point + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("Expected score with its measurement error band")
```

*"Given the score band: x is score, y is expected, a ribbon from lower to upper,
and also a line and points."*

The dash on that line comes from [`style(pattern = )`](../style.qmd). That
`style()` is written after `line`, so it belongs to that layer, and the band is
not dashed. On a stroke the texture is a **dash**. The band takes the same
setting, with different values. On a fill the
texture is a **hatch**: `"hatch"`, `"crosshatch"`, `"stripes"`, `"grid"` or
`"dots"`, never `"dashed"`.

## Filled, or two dashed edges {#filled-or-two-dashed-edges}

Some plots need the band without a fill. A band starts as a low and high pair,
and the *mark* decides how that pair is drawn. This follows the [No
Exceptions](../design-laws.qmd#law-2-no-exceptions) law. The same `bin` gives a
bar chart, a frequency polygon and a step histogram. In the same way, one pair
is drawn in four ways: as a whisker, filled, as two strokes, or as two
staircases. `ribbon`
**fills** the pair. A [`line`](line.qmd) traces its **two boundaries** instead,
which is the unfilled band many journals prefer.
With `style(pattern = )` it becomes the dashed pair of curves those journals
often print:

```{r}
data(score_band) + x(score) + y(expected) +
  line * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "gray", pattern = "dashed", size = 1.2) +
  line + style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  point + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("The same band, unfilled: two dashed edges")
```

*"Given the score band: x is score, y is expected, lines from lower to upper,
and also a line and points."*

`line * bounds` is one layer that draws *both* edges, splitting the pair into a
low curve and a high one. So you do not write one `y()` for the low edge and
another for the high edge. Two plain `line` layers can draw two columns you
already have. They cannot split a pair that `range` computes, because that pair
never becomes a column you can name. A `line` draws every pair transform the
same way. `line * range` traces the lowest and the highest values, and `line *
confidence` traces the two ends of a confidence interval.
[`step`](step.qmd) `* bounds` draws the same two edges as staircases. Filled or
unfilled, solid or dashed, it is one pair and a choice of mark, never a new
option added to the band.

Four marks draw a low and high pair: [`interval`](interval.qmd) draws it as a
whisker at each x, `line` and `step` trace its two boundaries, and `ribbon`
fills between them. All four marks draw `range`, `confidence`, `deviation`,
`smooth_band`, `straight_band` and `bounds`.

## One band per group {#one-band-per-group}

How does the spread of one continent compare with another's, year by year? The
`gm_continents` table holds every country of three continents (Asia, Europe and
the Americas), measured every five years from 1952 to 2007. One band per
continent puts all three spreads in one panel. A categorical column *splits* a
ribbon into one band per group. `color` splits the rows into one **series** per
continent, the rows that one band is drawn through, and `group` and `pattern`
split them the same way. It is the same split that gives [`area`](area.qmd) one region
per group and `line` one stroke per group. Here each continent gets its own
band, the range of its countries' life expectancy over time:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_continents)
```

```{r}
data(gm_continents) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Life expectancy spread, three continents")
```

*"Given the gapminder continents: ribbons derived by range, x is year, y is
life, color by continent."*

Europe's band narrows from about 29 years wide in 1952 to about 10 in 2007, and
the Americas' from 31 to 20. Asia's stays about 37 to 40 years wide, except for
a dip in its lower edge in 1977.

The bands overlap where two continents cover the same range of life expectancy.
A split `area` draws each region nearly opaque, as it draws a single one, so
little of the region behind shows through. For an area, `stack` solves this: it
starts each region at the top of the ones below, so no two regions overlap. A
ribbon split into groups draws each band translucent by default instead, so a
band behind another stays readable. The difference follows from what each mark
measures. An area measures a height from the baseline, so its groups can be
piled into a total. A ribbon already spans a low to a high and measures no such
height, so there is nothing to stack. Overlapping bands are read through
transparency and never stacked, which is why `ribbon * stack` is refused and the
refusal names `style(opacity = )`.

## One region, one fill {#one-region-one-fill}

The bands above are equally translucent, and each has its own color. Can you
map a column to a band's opacity instead? No, whether the column is a category
or a number. On a ribbon, `opacity` belongs to the layer, not to each band: every band in the
layer has the same opacity, exactly as on [`area`](area.qmd#one-region-one-fill).
So `opacity` is a *setting* here and not a channel. One band cannot be lighter
in one year and darker in another, and one continent's band cannot be lighter
than another's.

`color` is different, because it belongs to each band. A categorical column
gives each band its own color, as in the plot above. One band still has one
color, so a continuous column, which would change the color within a band, is
refused. [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows both refusals.

`size` is refused both ways: a ribbon neither maps it nor sets it. A band's
extent comes entirely from its x values and its two boundaries, so there is no
size to choose. To outline the band, layer a `line` along its
boundaries rather than setting an outline on the mark. The plot in [What you
can set](#what-you-can-set) does this with `line * bounds`.

## A category on the domain {#a-category-on-the-domain}

What happens when `x` holds categories instead of years? The spread of each
continent and its center can be drawn as one band across the categories. You
then see one shape across the panel, as with an area's filled profile. A
band's two axes do different jobs, as an area's do. The **domain** is the axis
the band runs along, and the **measure** is the axis its low and high are read
on. In every band so far the domain was `x`, holding years; here it holds
continents. A ribbon takes a
category on `x`, the same way an [`area`](area.qmd) does, and fills the spread
across the categories in the order they first appear in the table: Asia,
Europe, Africa, the Americas, Oceania. The `gapminder_2007` table holds one row
for each of 142 countries in 2007:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + line * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * range + line * mean: spread and center, per continent")
```

The band runs from each continent's lowest life expectancy to its highest, and
the line marks each continent's mean.

For most such data an [`interval`](interval.qmd) is the better sentence. It
draws a separate whisker at each category and claims nothing about the space
between them. A ribbon instead slopes from one category to the next, across
positions where no rows exist. The grammar does not decide that for you: both
sentences are well formed, and which one fits *your* data is a question about
the data.

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + interval * range + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("interval * range: the same numbers, claiming less")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: intervals derived by range, x is continent, y is life."*

Each whisker spans the same lowest and highest values as the band, and nothing
is drawn between the continents.

The band also turns down the page when the continents are on `y`, as [the
line's profile](line.qmd#the-profile-turned) does. It then spans each
continent's range along `x`:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + line * mean + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * range + line * mean + y(continent): the band, turned")
```

Asia's band is the widest, from 43.8 to 82.6 years, and Oceania's, with two
countries, is the narrowest.

## The violin: a distribution per category {#the-violin-a-distribution-per-category}

A `range` on a category gives two numbers per group, the lowest and the highest.
`density` gives a whole *shape* per group, and a ribbon can draw that shape.
With `density`, the category is no longer the domain. Each continent takes a
**slot**, the stretch of the axis that belongs to one category, and the curve
runs along the other axis, `y`. Its height at each life expectancy is drawn as
a width across the slot, on both sides, so the two halves
are the same curve facing opposite ways. That is the violin plot
[@hintze1998], and it is the band across the continents drawn above, with
`density` in place of `range` and without the line:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density, x is continent, y is life."*

`density` is not the ribbon's own transform. Five other marks draw the same
estimated curve, and only the shape changes. That is the [No
Exceptions](../design-laws.qmd#law-2-no-exceptions) law: a mark draws whatever
rows a transform returns, in the mark's own way.

| Mark derived by `density` | Shape |
|---|---|
| `line * density` | the curve as a stroke |
| `step * density` | the curve as a staircase |
| `area * density` | the curve filled to the baseline |
| `point * density` | one dot at each point the curve was estimated |
| `bar * density` | one thin bar at each of those points |
| `ribbon * density` | the curve mirrored, the violin above |

`line`, `step` and `area` also read a category on one axis, exactly as the
violin does. `point` and `bar` need a continuous axis instead: one dot or one
thin bar per estimated point cannot be read inside a category's slot, so gog
refuses both there.

Nothing new was added to the grammar to draw the violin. A ribbon closes on a
second boundary the data supplies, and a violin closes on the mirror image of
its own curve. `density` estimates a distribution, and this plot computes one
estimate for each group. There is no `violin` word to learn. Such a word would
have to say four things at once: the mark, the transform, the mirror and the
slot. The sentence already says all four: `ribbon` is the mark and supplies the
mirror, `density` is the transform, and the category on `x` gives the slot.

Compare it with the [`box`](box.qmd) drawn from the same two columns:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is continent, y is life."*

A box gives you five numbers you can name. The violin gives you the shape those
five numbers summarize. Africa's violin is widest near 52 years, and it has a
second, smaller bulge near 73. Africa's median is 53, and none of the box's five
numbers shows that second cluster.

### What the width means {#what-the-width-means}

Every group's density integrates to 1 on its own. If that were the whole
estimate, the widths would say nothing about how many rows each group has. A
continent of two countries would be drawn as large as a continent of fifty-two.
So by default the estimate is weighted by the group's row count, and width means
the same thing across the whole panel. Oceania holds two countries, so it is the
narrowest of the five violins.

The weighting is on the shape's **area**, the space it covers, not on its width,
which is why Europe's violin is wider than Africa's. Europe's thirty countries
differ in life expectancy by no more than ten years, so Europe's area is packed
into a short stretch of the axis and the shape has to be wide. Africa's
fifty-two countries cover thirty-seven years of life expectancy, so its larger
area is spread across a much longer stretch of the axis. What the width reports
at any height is countries per year of life expectancy, and that reading is the
same in every slot.

`compare = "shape"` removes that weighting and draws every violin to the same
area. It suits a question about the shapes alone. It misleads when a group
whose values are packed together is drawn so wide that every other violin is
drawn thin:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density(compare = "shape") + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title('density(compare = "shape"): every violin the same area')
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density compared by shape, x is
continent, y is life."*

Oceania is now the widest violin and Africa the thinnest, so two countries are
drawn wider than fifty-two. Oceania's two values are one year apart, so its
shape covers the shortest stretch of the axis. To hold the same area as the
others in that short stretch, it has to be the widest. The widest shape in a
panel sets the scale, so every other violin is drawn in proportion to it.
The two plots answer different questions. The default answers how many
countries lie at each life expectancy, and `compare = "shape"` answers how each
continent's values are spread, however many countries it holds. gog weights
each violin by its row count unless you write `compare = "shape"`.

### Compared with ggplot2's violin {#compared-with-ggplot2s-violin}

If you have used ggplot2, you will notice that gog's violins differ from those
`geom_violin()` draws on the same data. Three choices cause the difference, and
gog makes each one on purpose.

First, the ends narrow to a point. A violin is the density curve mirrored, and
gog draws the whole curve. The curve runs three bandwidths past each group's
smallest and largest value. The bandwidth is the width of the bell-shaped
kernel that `density` places on each value. No row in the table lies in these
tails. Oceania's two countries lie at 80.2 and 81.2 years, but with the
bandwidth of 2.04 years that all five violins share, its violin runs from 74.1
to 87.4. Split by `color(continent)`, `line * density` draws these same tails,
so the violin and the curve show one estimate. `geom_violin()` stops each
violin at its group's smallest and largest value, so its ends are flat. With
`trim = FALSE`, it draws tails the same way, three bandwidths long.

Second, each violin's area is weighted by its row count, as
[What the width means](#what-the-width-means) explains. `geom_violin()` draws
every violin to the same area, which is what `compare = "shape"` draws in gog.

Third, every violin in a plot is smoothed by one bandwidth, so a difference in
shape comes from the data and not from the smoothing
([One transform, four readings](../transforms.qmd#one-transform-four-readings)).
`geom_violin()` gives each violin its own bandwidth.

In gog, only the second choice can be changed to match `geom_violin()`. The
ends always narrow to a point, and every violin shares one bandwidth, whether
gog chooses it or you set it with `density(bandwidth = )` ([Choosing the
bandwidth](../transforms.qmd#choosing-the-bandwidth)).

### Sideways, and halved {#sideways-and-halved}

A violin turns as the band did in [A category on the
domain](#a-category-on-the-domain). Here `density` makes the category a slot,
and gog reads the orientation from the bindings, as it does for a
[`bar`](bar.qmd) or a [`box`](box.qmd). A category on
`y` is the form with room for long category names:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same violins, turned sideways")
```

An [`area`](area.qmd) draws the same estimate closed on the slot's center line
instead of on its mirror image. So `area` draws one half of the shape, and
`ribbon` draws both halves:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density: the half violin")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: areas derived by density, x is continent, y is life."*

There are two choices here, and they are made independently: which mark closes
the region, and which axis carries the category. That gives four plots. The one
this chapter has not drawn yet, an `area * density` with the category on `y`, has a name
of its own. Halve the violin *and* turn it sideways. Each category then gets a
filled curve rising from its slot's center line, above one shared measure axis.
That is the **ridgeline plot**, and each category's curve in it is a **ridge**:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density + x(life): the ridgeline")
```

Nothing was added for it either. It is the half violin's sentence with `x` and
`y` exchanged.

Read together, the four plots (the violin, the sideways violin, the half violin
and the ridgeline) show what
[orthogonality](../design-laws.qmd#law-1-orthogonality) gives you here. One
idea draws all four plots: `density` estimated per category, filled on one side
of the slot's center line or on both, with the category on either axis. A word
for the violin and a word for the ridgeline would name two of the four. The
other two would have no word, and neither would the idea behind all four.

### Letting the ridges overlap {#letting-the-ridges-overlap}

The ridgeline above keeps every ridge inside its own slot. That comes from how
far a shape reaches by default. The widest shape in a panel reaches `0.4` of a
slot from the slot's center line, and every other shape is drawn in proportion
to it. A slot ends `0.5` from that line, so each shape stays inside its own
slot, with empty space before the next category. [Bars](bar.qmd) follow the same
rule, for the same reason: the gap shows that the categories are separate
groups, not pieces of one continuous scale.

A ridgeline, as it is usually drawn, breaks that rule on purpose: its ridges are
tall enough to reach into the slot above, and the overlap is
intended. `density(reach = )` says how far, *in slots*:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * density(reach = 2.5) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("reach = 2.5: the tallest ridge two and a half slots tall")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: areas derived by density reaching 2.5 slots, x is life,
y is continent."*

The number is measured from the slot's center line to the shape's furthest
point. That is why the number means the same thing to both marks. A `ribbon`
reaches that far on each side, an `area` on one side only. The half violin
therefore stays exactly half of the violin, at any reach. Past `0.5` the shapes
leave their own slots. gog does not refuse this: a reach above `0.5` is unusual
but legal, so gog draws what your sentence asks for. Where two ridges overlap, the lower one is drawn
later and covers the one above it.

The categorical axis grows to hold the ridges. Normally the axis leaves half a slot
of space beyond the first and last categories, which is enough for a
[`bar`](bar.qmd) or a [`box`](box.qmd), since each stays inside its slot. A
ridge 2.5 slots tall does not stay in its slot, so the axis adds the room it
needs. Without that room, the panel edge would hide the top of the highest
ridge.

The edge is a layer here, as it was wherever this chapter drew a band's edge.
Neither `area` nor `ribbon` takes a border setting. A [`line`](line.qmd) given
the same transform traces the outline of the fill. That
is the [Filled, or two dashed edges](#filled-or-two-dashed-edges) rule again,
this time inside a category's slot:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.9) +
  line * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "black", size = 1) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same ridges, with their edges drawn")
```

Both layers read the same `density(reach = 2.5)`, so the stroke lies exactly on
the outline of the fill. That is why no border setting is needed: a layer draws
the outline, with its own color, width and dash. Color each ridge by its own
category and the plot is complete:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.2) + color(continent) +
  line * density(reach = 2.2) + style(color = "black", size = 0.9) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("One hue per ridge")
```

The `color(continent)` is written *after* the area, so it belongs to that layer
alone. Written before both marks, it would also reach the `line`, whose
`style(color = "black")` sets the color. One layer cannot both map a channel and
set it, so gog would refuse the sentence. The place where a channel
is written in the sentence decides its scope, and [Encoding
scope](../encoding-scope.qmd#channels-plot-scoped-or-layer-scoped)
explains that in full.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a ribbon takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("ribbon")
```

The plots below show every transform a ribbon takes. Within a figure the plots
differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any
other change. The six pair transforms, `density` and `flow` are marked ●: a
ribbon cannot draw without one of them. [Why a ribbon needs a
transform](#why-a-ribbon-needs-a-transform) explains this for the pairs and
`density`. For `flow`, the
[`flow`](../transforms.qmd#flow-a-magnitude-through-its-stages) section of
Transforms shows the bands it gives a ribbon.

**Counting.** `density` is the one counting transform a ribbon takes. For each
category, it estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely the rows lie along the
number axis. So it needs a category on one axis and a number on the other. The
ribbon draws each curve and its mirror image across the category's slot, and the
shape is the violin. Without a category, `density` gives one curve, which is
only one edge, so the ribbon refuses it. The category can be on either axis:

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
   title("ribbon * density")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(life) + y(continent) +
     title("ribbon * density"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density, x is continent, y is life,
beside ribbons derived by density, x is life, y is continent."*

**Pairs.** The pair transforms give `y` a low and a high at each value of `x`,
and the ribbon fills the band between them. `range`, `confidence` and
`deviation` reduce the rows at each value of `x`, so they need a number on `y`.
`range` gives the smallest and the largest value. `confidence` gives the 95%
confidence interval of the mean, and `deviation` reaches one standard deviation
from the mean on each side. `smooth_band` and `straight_band` need a number on
each axis. They fit a line to the rows, each placed at its `x` and its `y`.
They then give a low and a high around that line at 100 evenly spaced places
along `x`, or as many as `places` sets. `bounds` computes
nothing: it reads the low and the high from two columns you name, and it needs
no `y`. Five plots read the `gm_all` table, shown in [A fan chart of nested
bands](#a-fan-chart-of-nested-bands). The sixth reads the `score_band` table,
shown in [A pre-computed band](#a-pre-computed-band), with `score` on `x`:

```{r}
((data(gm_all) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) +
    title("ribbon * range")) |
  (data(gm_all) + ribbon * confidence + x(year) + y(life) +
     title("ribbon * confidence")) |
  (data(gm_all) + ribbon * deviation + x(year) + y(life) +
     title("ribbon * deviation"))) /
  ((data(gm_all) + ribbon * smooth_band + x(year) + y(life) +
      title("ribbon * smooth_band")) |
     (data(gm_all) + ribbon * straight_band + x(year) + y(life) +
        title("ribbon * straight_band")) |
     (data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + x(score) +
        title("ribbon * bounds")))
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: a ribbon derived by range, x is year, y is
life, beside a ribbon derived by confidence, x is year, y is life, beside a
ribbon derived by deviation, x is year, y is life; above a ribbon derived by
smooth_band, x is year, y is life, beside a ribbon derived by straight_band, x
is year, y is life, beside a ribbon from the score band, from lower to upper, x
is score."*

The five plots that read `life` share one scale, so the widths of their bands
can be compared. The range is the widest band. Its lower edge is the single
lowest country in each year, so it drops in 1977 and in 1992. The confidence
band is about 4 years wide in every year, because a mean computed from 142
values has little uncertainty.

**Layouts.** `flow` follows an amount from one stage to the next. Each stage is
a categorical column, named inside `flow()`. The ribbon draws one band for each
combination of categories across the stages, as thick as the amount in that
combination. The amount is the column on `y`, and without one every row counts
as 1. A `zone` and a `text` layer given the same `flow` draw the slots at each
stage and their names, as the [Flow](../flow.qmd) chapter shows. The `titanic` table counts the
people on board by class, sex, age and whether they survived, so `y(n)` sums
those counts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(titanic)
```

```{r}
data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, survived) + color(class) +
  zone * flow(class, survived) +
  text * flow(class, survived) +
  title("ribbon * flow, with zones and names")
```

*"Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class and survived,
colored by class, and also zones derived by flow through class and survived,
and also text derived by flow through class and survived."*

The widest band goes from `Crew` to `No`: 673 of the 885 crew did not survive.

A ribbon refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. `bin`, `count`,
`proportion`, the summaries, the fitted lines and the running total give one
number at each value of `x`, and a band needs two edges. An [`area`](area.qmd)
fills one value down to the baseline, and a [`line`](line.qmd) draws it as a
stroke. A ribbon takes no collision modifier: gog never moves a band aside or piles one
band on another. Bands that share a place overlap instead, even two violins
split by color in one slot, and a ribbon draws each band translucent, so a band
behind another still shows, as [One band per group](#one-band-per-group)
explains. `jitter` moves
each point a short way along the categorical axis, and `repel` moves
[`text`](text.qmd) labels. `partition` and `cluster` lay out rectangles and
branches, which [`zone`](zone.qmd) and [`path`](path.qmd) draw. `layout` places
a network, which [`point`](point.qmd), [`text`](text.qmd) and
[`edge`](edge.qmd) draw.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

A setting changes how the band looks without reading a column, and each mark
takes its own. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are a ribbon's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("ribbon")
```

A ribbon takes `area`'s list, and for `area`'s reasons. There is no `size`,
because the band's shape comes from the two boundaries its transform supplies.
There is no border, because the edge is a `line` traced along the same pair.

One setting this chapter has not shown on a band is a fill `pattern`. Here is a
band hatched with a grid, with a dashed `line` along both of its boundaries. The
plot uses the `score_band` table, shown in
[A pre-computed band](#a-pre-computed-band):

```{r}
data(score_band) + x(score) +
  ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) +
    style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "grid", opacity = 0.45) +
  line * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Expected true score") + title("A textured band, and its two edges")
```

*"Given the score band: x is score, a ribbon from lower to upper, with pattern
grid, and also lines from lower to upper, with pattern dashed."*

Both marks read the same `bounds(lower, upper)` there, exactly as the two ridge
layers did, so the edges stay on the band. The two `pattern` values follow the
rule from [A pre-computed band](#a-pre-computed-band): a hatch on the fill, a
dash on the stroke.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

gog refuses five kinds of ribbon sentence: a category on both axes, a ribbon
with no transform to supply its two boundaries, a mapped `opacity` or a
continuous `color`, any `size`, and a split that leaves one position in every
series. The first refusal comes from the measure. A band from `range` spans a low
value to a high one, and both are quantities, so one axis must hold a
continuous column. With categories on both axes there is nothing to span:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(continent) + y(country)
```

A category on one axis alone is accepted, on either axis. On `y`, beside a
number on `x`, the band turns down the page and spans each category's low and high along `x`, as
[the profile](line.qmd#the-profile-turned) does in Line. With `density`, the
violins above use a category on `y` as a slot instead.

A bare `ribbon` is the second refusal. A plain `y()` supplies one number, and a
band needs two boundaries, as [Why a ribbon needs a
transform](#why-a-ribbon-needs-a-transform) explained. The engine says so
rather than drawing an empty panel:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon + x(year) + y(life)
```

The message names two of the six pair transforms, `range` and `bounds`, and
shows how to write each.

A mapped `opacity` or a continuous `color` is the third. A ribbon's opacity
belongs to the layer, and its color to each band, as [One region, one
fill](#one-region-one-fill) explains. The message for `opacity` names
`style(opacity = )`:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) + opacity(gdp)
```

A categorical column gives each band its own color. A continuous column on
`color` is refused, because one band has one color:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) + color(gdp)
```

A `size` is the fourth, and it is refused both ways. A band's extent comes from
its x values and its two boundaries, so there is no size to map and none to
set:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) + style(size = 3)
```

The fifth refusal comes from the series. A band needs at least two positions
along its domain in each series, each with a low and a high value. Split by
`color(continent)`, each continent's series holds one position, so the plot
would draw nothing, and gog refuses it. The message suggests
`interval * range`, which draws each position on its own:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(continent) + y(life) +
  color(continent)
```

## In short {#in-short}

A ribbon fills the space between two boundaries, and refuses to draw until a
transform supplies them. The transform decides what the band means: the
extremes from `range`, the middle from two quantiles, the mean's uncertainty
from `confidence`, and a band computed elsewhere from `bounds`. Over a category,
`density` makes the ribbon a violin. Both edges come from the data, so the
band's shape is never a setting. `opacity` belongs to the layer, and `color` to
each band.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

A ribbon shows a region and names nothing inside it. [Text](text.qmd) draws a
string at each position, read from a column.
